html:
Every page you have ever opened — the NEB result page, a school website, a news site — is a plain text file with tags in it. That is the whole secret of this unit. HTML is not a programming language and there is nothing to compile: you type text, you wrap it in tags, you save it with a .html extension, and a browser turns it into a page. This unit takes you from what the web is to writing, styling and publishing a page of your own.

What the examiner wants from this unit

The NEB paper asks for tags with their attributes, written correctly. You will be asked to write HTML code for a given output — usually a table, a form or a list — so practise writing tags by hand, not by copying. Learn the difference between a tag and an attribute, between HTML and HTTP, and between the three ways of attaching CSS. Every tag you write in the exam must be spelt correctly and closed correctly.

6.1 Web development, web browsers and search engines

Web development

Web development is the work of building and maintaining websites — designing the pages, writing the code, putting the site on a server and keeping it running. It is usually split into front-end work (what the visitor sees: HTML, CSS and JavaScript running in the browser) and back-end work (what happens on the server: PHP, Python, databases).

A web page is a single document. A website is a collection of related web pages kept under one domain name. The first page a visitor lands on is the home page.

Web browser

A web browser is application software that requests a web page from a web server, interprets the HTML, CSS and JavaScript it receives, and displays the result. Examples: Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge, Safari, Opera.

The part of a browser that turns HTML into pixels is called the rendering engine — Blink in Chrome and Edge, Gecko in Firefox, WebKit in Safari.

Search engine

A search engine is a website that maintains an index of other web pages and returns a list of the ones matching a user's query. Examples: Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo, Yahoo.

A search engine works in three stages. A crawler (or spider) follows links from page to page collecting documents; an indexer stores the words of every page it finds in a huge index; and when you type a query the query processor searches that index and ranks the hits so the most relevant come first. So when you search, you are not searching the web — you are searching a copy of it that the search engine made earlier.

A browser and a search engine are not the same thing. The browser is software installed on your device; the search engine is a website you visit using a browser.

6.2 The internet, web technologies and content management systems

The internet is the global network of interconnected computer networks. The World Wide Web (WWW) is just one of the services that runs on it — a collection of linked documents identified by URLs and fetched using HTTP. Email, FTP and video calls are other internet services that are not the Web. Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989.

Internet vs WWW

The internet is the road network; the web is the traffic of documents travelling on it. There are other kinds of traffic on the same roads.

The core technologies you must know by name:

Technology Stands for Does what
HTML HyperText Markup Language gives a page its structure
CSS Cascading Style Sheets gives a page its presentation
JavaScript — gives a page its behaviour
HTTP / HTTPS HyperText Transfer Protocol (Secure) the rules for requesting and sending pages
URL Uniform Resource Locator the address of a page
FTP File Transfer Protocol uploading a site to the server

The web works on the client–server model. Your browser is the client; it sends an HTTP request; the web server sends back an HTTP response containing the HTML file and everything the page needs.

Content Management System (CMS)

A Content Management System is software that lets people create, edit, organise and publish content on a website without writing HTML. The content is stored in a database and poured into ready-made page templates.

Popular examples are WordPress, Joomla and Drupal. A CMS separates three jobs: the content (in the database), the template or theme (the look), and the plugins or extensions (extra features such as a photo gallery or a contact form). That is why a school office clerk can add a notice to the school website without knowing a single tag.

Advantages of a CMS: no coding needed to publish content; several people can work on the same site with different permission levels; the look can be changed by switching the theme without touching the content; updates and backups are built in. Disadvantages: the site is heavier and slower than hand-written HTML; you depend on plugin authors; an unpatched CMS is a common target for attackers.

6.3 HTML: objectives, structure, publishing and hosting

HTML

HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard markup language used to create the structure of web pages. HyperText means text that contains links to other text; markup means the content is marked with tags that say what each part of it is. HTML was created by Tim Berners-Lee in 1991; the current version is HTML5 (2014).

HTML is not a programming language — it has no variables, no conditions and no loops. It describes a document; it does not compute anything.

Objectives of HTML — to structure the content of a page (headings, paragraphs, lists, tables); to link documents to one another through hyperlinks; to embed images, audio and video; and to present forms that collect data from the visitor. Being plain text, an HTML file is platform independent: the same file displays on Windows, Linux, Android and iOS.

Every HTML document has the same skeleton.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>My First Web Page</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Namaste from Nepal</h1>
  <p>This is my first web page.</p>
</body>
</html>
  • <!DOCTYPE html> tells the browser this is an HTML5 document. It is a declaration, not a tag.
  • <html> is the root element; everything else lives inside it.
  • <head> holds information about the page — title, character set, links to stylesheets. Nothing in the head appears in the page body.
  • <title> sets the text shown on the browser tab and used by search engines. It is compulsory.
  • <body> holds everything the visitor actually sees.

Tags versus attributes. A tag is the keyword in angle brackets that names an element — <p>, <img>, <table>. Most tags come in pairs: an opening tag <p> and a closing tag </p>. A few are empty (or void) tags that have no closing partner, such as <br>, <hr>, <img> and <meta>.

An attribute is extra information written inside the opening tag as name="value", which modifies the element.

<img src="everest.jpg" alt="Mount Everest" width="300">

Here img is the tag and src, alt and width are three attributes. An attribute never appears in a closing tag.

Tag Attribute
Written in angle brackets inside the opening tag
Job names the element modifies the element
Form <p> … </p> name="value"
Compulsory? yes, an element is its tag no, most are optional

Publishing and hosting. Writing the file is only half the job. To publish it:

  1. Create the pages in a text editor (Notepad, Notepad++, VS Code) and save with a .html extension.
  2. Test every page locally by opening it in a browser.
  3. Buy or register a domain name (§6.13).
  4. Buy space on a web server — this is web hosting.
  5. Upload the files to the server using FTP software such as FileZilla, or the hosting control panel (cPanel).
  6. Test the live site and keep it updated.
HTML is forgiving — and that is the trap

If you misspell a tag or forget a closing tag, the browser does not show an error. It silently guesses, and the page comes out wrong somewhere you did not expect. There is no compiler to catch your mistakes, so check your own tags, and close every element you open.

6.4 Basic tags: HTML, HEAD, TITLE and BODY

The four structural tags were shown in §6.3. The <body> tag carries the attributes that control the look of the whole page.

Attribute of <body> Controls Example
bgcolor background colour bgcolor="#fff8e7"
text foreground (text) colour text="#003366"
background background image background="paper.png"
link vlink alink unvisited, visited and active link colours link="blue"

A colour is written either as a name (red, navy, orange) or as a hexadecimal code #RRGGBB, two hex digits each for red, green and blue. So #FF0000 is pure red, #000000 is black and #FFFFFF is white.

Background sound was set by the <bgsound> tag, which only ever worked in Internet Explorer:

<body bgcolor="#fff8e7" text="#003366" background="paper.png">
  <bgsound src="music.mid" loop="infinite">
These presentation attributes are obsolete

bgcolor, text, background, align, <font>, <basefont> and <bgsound> are all removed from HTML5. They are in your syllabus and the board may ask for them, so learn them — but know that a validator rejects them. Running the code above through the HTML Tidy validator gives, word for word:

Warning: <body> attribute "background" not allowed for HTML5
Warning: <body> attribute "bgcolor" not allowed for HTML5
Warning: <body> attribute "text" not allowed for HTML5
Warning: <h1> attribute "align" not allowed for HTML5
Warning: <basefont> element removed from HTML5
Warning: <font> element removed from HTML5
Warning: <bgsound> is not approved by W3C

The modern replacement for every one of them is CSS (§6.14), and for background sound it is the HTML5 <audio> element (§6.11).

The HTML5 way to do the same thing is one line of CSS:

body { background-color: #fff8e7; color: #003366;
       background-image: url("paper.png"); }

6.5 Heading tags and the FONT tag

HTML has six levels of heading, <h1> down to <h6>. <h1> is the largest and most important, <h6> the smallest. Headings are not just big text: search engines and screen readers use them to work out the structure of the page, so use one <h1> per page and go down in order.

<h1 align="center">Heading level 1</h1>
<h2 align="left">Heading level 2</h2>
<h3>Heading level 3</h3>
<h4>Heading level 4</h4>
<h5>Heading level 5</h5>
<h6>Heading level 6</h6>

The align attribute takes left (the default), center, right or justify. In HTML5 it is replaced by style="text-align:center".

The <font> tag used to control the appearance of text and has three attributes:

Attribute Values Meaning
size 1 to 7 1 is smallest, 3 is the default, 7 is largest
color name or #RRGGBB colour of the text
face font name(s) typeface, e.g. Arial, Helvetica

<basefont size="4"> set a default size for the rest of the page. A size can also be given relative to the base: size="+2" means two steps larger.

<basefont size="4">
<font size="5" color="red" face="Arial">Big red Arial text</font>
<p>Normal text, then <small>small text</small> and <big>big text</big>.</p>

<small> renders one step smaller and <big> one step larger than the surrounding text. <small> survives in HTML5 (it now means fine print, like a copyright line); <big> was removed — the Tidy validator reports Warning: <big> element removed from HTML5. The CSS replacement for the whole <font> tag is:

p { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; font-size: 18px; color: navy; }

6.6 Paragraphs, line breaks and comments

A browser collapses every run of spaces, tabs and newlines in your source into a single space. Pressing Enter in the editor does nothing to the page. You must say where paragraphs and lines end with tags.

  • <p> … </p> marks a paragraph. Browsers put blank space above and below it. align works here too.
  • <br> forces a line break inside a paragraph. It is an empty tag with no closing partner (you may write <br />).
  • <hr> draws a horizontal rule — a dividing line. Also an empty tag.
<p>First line<br>Second line after a break.</p>
<hr>
<p align="justify">A justified paragraph.</p>

A comment is a note for the author that the browser ignores completely:

<!-- This is a comment. The browser does not display it. -->

Comments explain sections of a long page and are also used to temporarily switch off a piece of code while testing. They may run over several lines, but they may not be nested inside one another.

6.7 Formatting text

These tags change how a run of text looks or what it means.

Tag Effect Example source Shows as
<b> bold <b>Bold</b> Bold
<i> italic <i>italic</i> italic
<u> underline <u>Under</u> Under, underlined
<mark> highlighted, like a marker pen <mark>note</mark> note on yellow
<sup> superscript, raised and smaller 5<sup>2</sup> 5²
<sub> subscript, lowered and smaller H<sub>2</sub>O H₂O
<em> emphasis — italic with meaning <em>must</em> must
<strong> strong importance — bold with meaning <strong>Stop</strong> Stop
<blockquote> a long quotation, indented on both sides — indented block
<pre> preformatted — keeps every space and newline, in a monospaced font — text as typed

<b> and <i> are presentational — they say "make it look bold". <strong> and <em> are semantic — they say "this matters", and a screen reader will change its tone of voice for them. They look identical on screen.

<pre> is the one tag that switches off the whitespace-collapsing rule, which makes it the right tag for program code and for tables of figures typed by hand.

<p><b>Bold</b>, <i>italic</i>, <u>underlined</u>,
   <mark>highlighted</mark>, <em>emphasised</em>,
   <strong>strong</strong>.</p>
<p>H<sub>2</sub>O is water and 5<sup>2</sup> is 25.</p>
<blockquote cite="https://www.neb.gov.np">
  A quotation is indented from both sides by the browser.
</blockquote>
<pre>
Roll   Name         Marks
  1    Sushmita       82
  2    Bibek          74
</pre>

6.8 Lists: ordered, unordered and definition

An ordered list numbers its items automatically. <ol> opens it and each item is an <li>.

Attribute On Values
type <ol> 1 (default), A, a, I, i
start <ol> the number the list starts at
value <li> forces this item's number, and renumbers the rest from there
reversed <ol> counts downwards

An unordered list <ul> puts a bullet in front of each item instead of a number. The bullet shape used to be set by type="disc" (the default, a filled circle), type="circle" (hollow) or type="square". In HTML5 this is style="list-style-type:square".

<ol type="I" start="3">
  <li>Kathmandu</li>
  <li value="7">Pokhara</li>
  <li>Biratnagar</li>
</ol>

That list displays as III. Kathmandu, then VII. Pokhara — because value="7" overrides the count — then VIII. Biratnagar, which continues from 7, not from IV.

Lists can be nested: put a whole <ul> inside an <li> of another list.

<ul style="list-style-type:square">
  <li>Input unit</li>
  <li>Processing unit
    <ul style="list-style-type:circle">
      <li>ALU</li>
      <li>CU</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>Output unit</li>
</ul>

A definition list (also called a description list) pairs terms with their meanings. It uses three tags: <dl> for the list, <dt> for the term and <dd> for the definition, which the browser indents.

<dl>
  <dt>HTML</dt>
  <dd>HyperText Markup Language, used to structure a web page.</dd>
  <dt>CSS</dt>
  <dd>Cascading Style Sheets, used to present a web page.</dd>
</dl>

6.9 The ADDRESS tag, links and the anchor tag

<address> marks up contact information for the author or owner of a page. Browsers show it in italics as a block.

<address>
  NEBians, Sanothimi, Bhaktapur<br>
  Email: <a href="mailto:info@example.com.np">info@example.com.np</a>
</address>

A hyperlink is text or an image that takes you somewhere else when clicked. It is made with the anchor tag <a>, whose essential attribute is href (hypertext reference) — the destination.

<a href="https://moecdc.gov.np">Curriculum Development Centre</a>

The text between <a> and </a> is what the visitor sees and clicks.

Attribute Meaning
href the URL or file the link points to
target where to open it: _blank (new tab), _self (same tab, default)
title tooltip text shown on hovering
id names a point in the page so links can jump to it

There are three kinds of link by destination:

  • External link — to another website: href="https://neb.gov.np".
  • Internal link — to another page of the same site, using a relative path: href="unit06.html" for a file in the same folder, href="notes/unit07.html" for one in a sub-folder.
  • Bookmark (same-page) link — to a named point on the page, using #: href="#summary" jumps to the element whose id is summary.

An email link uses the mailto: scheme and opens the visitor's mail program. An image link is made by putting an <img> between the anchor tags.

<p><a href="https://neb.gov.np" target="_blank">Open NEB in a new tab</a></p>
<p><a href="#summary">Jump to the summary on this page</a></p>
<p><a href="index.html"><img src="logo.png" alt="Home" width="80"></a></p>
<h2 id="summary">Summary</h2>
Worked example 6.1 — a complete personal page

Problem. Write the HTML for a page titled "My Village" with a centred heading, a short paragraph, a bulleted list of three places, and a link to the NEB website that opens in a new tab.

Solution.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>My Village</title>
</head>
<body bgcolor="#fffdf5" text="#222222">
  <h1 align="center">My Village</h1>
  <p align="justify">My village lies in the hills of Kaski district,
     about two hours' walk from the nearest road head.</p>
  <h2>Places to see</h2>
  <ul type="square">
    <li>The old temple</li>
    <li>The suspension bridge</li>
    <li>The viewpoint above the school</li>
  </ul>
  <hr>
  <address>Written by a Grade 11 student, 2082 BS</address>
  <p><a href="https://neb.gov.np" target="_blank" title="Exam board">
     National Examination Board</a></p>
</body>
</html>

Every element that was opened has been closed, and in the reverse order to the one in which it was opened. The empty tags <meta>, <hr> and <br> have no closing partner.

6.10 Tables and forms

A table arranges data in rows and columns. Three tags build it:

  • <table> … </table> encloses the whole table.
  • <tr> … </tr> is one table row.
  • <th> is a header cell — bold and centred by default.
  • <td> is an ordinary data cell.

Cells go inside rows, and rows go inside the table — never the other way round.

Attribute On Meaning
border <table> thickness of the border lines
cellpadding <table> space between a cell's content and its edge
cellspacing <table> space between neighbouring cells
colspan <td> <th> how many columns this cell stretches across
rowspan <td> <th> how many rows this cell stretches down
align <table> <tr> <td> horizontal alignment of the content

<caption> placed immediately after <table> gives the table a title.

Worked example 6.2 — a marks table

Problem. Write the HTML for a table with the heading row Roll, Name, Computer, two data rows, and a final row where the word "Average" spans the first two columns.

Solution.

<table border="1" cellpadding="5">
  <caption>Marks of Grade 11</caption>
  <tr>
    <th>Roll</th><th>Name</th><th>Computer</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>1</td><td>Sushmita</td><td>82</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>2</td><td>Bibek</td><td>74</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td colspan="2">Average</td><td>78</td>
  </tr>
</table>

The last row has only two <td> tags, not three, because the first one covers two columns. Count the cells in every row: a row whose colspan values do not add up to the number of columns produces a ragged table.

A form collects data from the visitor and sends it to a program on the server. <form> encloses the controls and carries two attributes: action (the server program that will receive the data) and method (get, which puts the data in the URL, or post, which hides it in the request body — use post for passwords).

Control Written as
Text box <input type="text" name="sname" size="25">
Password box <input type="password" name="pw">
Radio button (choose one) <input type="radio" name="gender" value="m">
Check box (choose many) <input type="checkbox" name="sub" value="cs">
Multi-line text area <textarea name="addr" rows="3" cols="30"></textarea>
Drop-down list <select name="city"><option>Pokhara</option></select>
Submit button <input type="submit" value="Register">
Reset button <input type="reset" value="Clear">

The rule that catches most students: radio buttons in the same group must share the same name. That shared name is what makes them mutually exclusive. Check boxes that share a name are still independent of each other.

Worked example 6.3 — a registration form

Problem. Design a form that collects a name, a gender chosen from two radio buttons, one or more subjects chosen from check boxes, and an address, with Register and Clear buttons.

Solution.

<form action="register.php" method="post">
  <p>Name: <input type="text" name="sname" size="25"></p>
  <p>Gender:
    <input type="radio" name="gender" value="m" id="m"><label for="m">Male</label>
    <input type="radio" name="gender" value="f" id="f"><label for="f">Female</label>
  </p>
  <p>Subjects:
    <input type="checkbox" name="sub" value="cs" id="cs"><label for="cs">Computer</label>
    <input type="checkbox" name="sub" value="ph" id="ph"><label for="ph">Physics</label>
  </p>
  <p>Address:<br>
    <textarea name="addr" rows="3" cols="30"></textarea></p>
  <p>
    <input type="submit" value="Register">
    <input type="reset" value="Clear">
  </p>
</form>

Both radio buttons carry name="gender", so clicking one clears the other. The <textarea> needs a closing tag even when it is empty, unlike <input>, which is an empty tag.

6.11 HTML5 media elements: audio, video, source, track and embed

Before HTML5, playing sound or video needed a plug-in such as Flash. HTML5 gave the browser two built-in players.

<audio> plays sound; <video> plays moving pictures. Both take the attribute controls (show the play/pause bar), and also accept autoplay, loop, muted and preload. <video> additionally takes width, height and poster (a still image shown before play starts).

<source> is an empty tag placed inside <audio> or <video>. You give one <source> per file format; the browser plays the first one it understands and ignores the rest. This matters because no single format works everywhere — MP3 and MP4 are the widely supported pair, OGG and WebM the open alternatives.

<track> adds a timed text file (WebVTT, .vtt) to a video: subtitles, captions or chapter names. Its kind says which, srclang gives the language and default selects it automatically.

Any text typed between the opening and closing media tags is fallback content — shown only by a browser too old to support the element.

<audio controls>
  <source src="song.mp3" type="audio/mpeg">
  <source src="song.ogg" type="audio/ogg">
  Your browser does not support the audio element.
</audio>

<video width="480" height="270" controls poster="thumb.jpg">
  <source src="lesson.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  <source src="lesson.webm" type="video/webm">
  <track src="lesson-en.vtt" kind="subtitles" srclang="en" label="English" default>
  Your browser does not support the video element.
</video>

<embed> is the general-purpose container for external content handled by a plug-in or by the browser itself — a PDF, a map, a video from another site. It is an empty tag.

<embed src="notes.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="480" height="320">

6.12 HTML5 graphics: canvas and SVG

HTML5 can draw pictures in the page itself, in two completely different ways.

<canvas> is a rectangular drawing surface. The tag alone draws nothing — it is a blank sheet, and you paint on it with JavaScript. The result is a grid of pixels (a bitmap), so enlarging it makes it blurry, and once drawn, the browser no longer knows a rectangle is there.

<canvas id="myCanvas" width="200" height="120"
        style="border:1px solid #888"></canvas>
<script>
  var c = document.getElementById("myCanvas");
  var ctx = c.getContext("2d");
  ctx.fillStyle = "#3b6ea5";
  ctx.fillRect(20, 20, 120, 60);
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.arc(160, 50, 25, 0, 2 * Math.PI);
  ctx.stroke();
</script>

getContext("2d") hands back the drawing toolbox; fillRect(x, y, width, height) paints a solid rectangle; arc(x, y, r, start, end) traces a circle, and stroke() draws its outline.

SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) takes the opposite approach. Each shape is its own element in the document tree, written as a tag with attributes, so the browser keeps knowing it is a circle. Being described by coordinates rather than pixels, SVG stays perfectly sharp at any size, and each shape can be styled with CSS or given a click handler.

<svg width="200" height="120">
  <rect x="20" y="20" width="120" height="60" fill="#3b6ea5"></rect>
  <circle cx="160" cy="50" r="25" fill="none" stroke="black"></circle>
  <text x="20" y="105" font-size="14">Drawn with SVG</text>
</svg>

Both blocks above draw the same picture: a filled blue rectangle and an open circle beside it.

Canvas SVG
Kind of graphic raster (pixels) vector (shapes)
Drawn by JavaScript code HTML-like tags
On enlarging becomes blurry stays sharp
Individual shapes forgotten after drawing remain in the document tree
Suits games, charts with thousands of points logos, icons, maps, diagrams

6.13 Domain names and web hosting

Every computer on the internet is identified by an IP address, a number such as 142.250.183.4. Numbers are hard to remember, so we use names.

Domain name

A domain name is the unique, human-readable address of a website, such as neb.gov.np. The Domain Name System (DNS) is the internet service that translates a domain name into the IP address of the server that holds the site.

A domain name is read right to left, from the most general part to the most specific.

Common top-level domains (TLDs): .com (commercial), .org (organisation), .net (network), .edu (education), .gov (government), .info, .biz. Country-code TLDs identify a country: .np for Nepal, .in for India, .uk for the United Kingdom. Nepal's .np registry is administered by Mercantile Communication Pvt. Ltd., which takes registrations at the third level under second-level domains such as .com.np, .org.np, .net.np, .edu.np (schools, colleges and universities) and .gov.np (government bodies, overseen by the National Information Technology Centre). Registration under .np is free of cost, but the applicant must prove eligibility with citizenship or organisation registration documents.

For most TLDs a domain name is not bought outright — it is registered and rented from a registrar, normally for a year at a time, and must be renewed.

Web hosting

Web hosting is the service of storing a website's files on a web server that is permanently connected to the internet, so that anyone can request them at any time. The company that provides the service is a web host.

Type of hosting What you get Suits
Shared one server's resources divided among many sites small sites, school sites; cheapest
VPS (virtual private server) a guaranteed slice of a server, with root access growing sites
Dedicated a whole physical server to yourself large, busy sites; most expensive
Cloud resources spread over many servers, paid by use sites with changing traffic

A domain name and hosting are two separate purchases. The domain is the address; the hosting is the land and building. The domain is pointed at the hosting by setting its name servers in the registrar's control panel.

6.14 Cascading Style Sheets: inline, embedded and external

CSS

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is the language that describes how HTML elements should be presented — colour, size, spacing, position and typeface. HTML holds the structure; CSS holds the look. "Cascading" refers to the rules the browser follows when more than one style applies to the same element.

A CSS rule has two parts: a selector naming the elements it applies to, and a declaration block in braces holding property: value; pairs.

h1 { color: navy; text-align: center; }

Here h1 is the selector, color and text-align are properties, navy and center their values. Selectors you must know: the element selector (p), the class selector (.note, matching class="note", reusable on many elements) and the id selector (#header, matching id="header", used once per page).

There are three ways to attach CSS to a page.

1. Inline CSS — a style attribute on a single tag. It styles that one element only. Quick, but it mixes presentation into the structure and cannot be reused, so it is the worst method for a real site.

<p style="color: green">Inline CSS styled only this paragraph.</p>

2. Embedded (internal) CSS — a <style> element inside <head>. Its rules apply to every matching element on that page.

<head>
  <style>
    body  { background-color: #f4f4f4; font-family: Arial, sans-serif; }
    h1    { color: navy; text-align: center; }
    .note { border-left: 4px solid orange; padding-left: 10px; }
  </style>
</head>

3. External CSS — the rules live in a separate .css file with no HTML tags in it at all, and every page links to it with a <link> tag in its <head>.

<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">

This is the method professionals use: change one line of style.css and a hundred pages change at once, and the browser caches the file so the site loads faster.

When two rules apply to the same element, the more specific one wins: inline beats embedded, embedded beats external, and an id selector beats a class selector, which beats an element selector.

Worked example 6.4 — one page, all three methods

Problem. Write a page whose heading is navy and centred (embedded), whose background is light grey (embedded), that also links to style.css (external), and which has one green paragraph styled inline.

Solution.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Three ways to attach CSS</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
  <style>
    body  { background-color: #f4f4f4; font-family: Arial, sans-serif; }
    h1    { color: navy; text-align: center; }
    .note { border-left: 4px solid orange; padding-left: 10px; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Embedded CSS styled this heading</h1>
  <p class="note">External and embedded rules both reach this paragraph.</p>
  <p style="color: green">Inline CSS styled only this paragraph.</p>
</body>
</html>

The <link> tag is empty — no closing partner — and must sit inside <head>. If style.css also contained h1 { color: red; }, the heading would still come out navy, because the embedded rule is more specific than the external one.

Chapter summary

  • The internet is the network; the World Wide Web is one service running on it. A browser is software on your device; a search engine is a website that indexes other sites using a crawler, an indexer and a ranking step.
  • The web uses the client–server model: DNS turns the name into an IP address, the browser sends an HTTP request, the server sends an HTTP response with the HTML.
  • A CMS (WordPress, Joomla, Drupal) stores content in a database and pours it into templates, so people can publish without writing HTML.
  • HTML structures a page, CSS presents it, JavaScript gives it behaviour. HTML is a markup language, not a programming language.
  • Every document has <!DOCTYPE html>, <html>, <head> (with the compulsory <title>) and <body>. A tag names an element; an attribute (name="value") sits inside the opening tag and modifies it. <br>, <hr>, <img>, <meta>, <link> and <source> are empty tags.
  • Headings run <h1> (largest) to <h6>. <font size="1..7"> defaulted to 3. bgcolor, text, background, align, <font>, <basefont>, <big> and <bgsound> are all obsolete in HTML5 — CSS replaces them.
  • Browsers collapse whitespace, so paragraphs need <p> and line breaks need <br>. <pre> is the exception that preserves spacing.
  • <ol> numbers items (type, start, value); <ul> bullets them; <dl> with <dt> and <dd> defines terms.
  • The anchor tag <a href="..."> makes external, internal, bookmark (#id), email (mailto:) and image links; target="_blank" opens a new tab.
  • Tables are <table> → <tr> → <th> or <td>, with colspan and rowspan merging cells. Forms use <input> with type set to text, radio, checkbox, submit or reset, plus <textarea>; radio buttons in one group share a name.
  • HTML5 media: <audio> and <video> with controls, several <source> files for different formats, <track> for subtitles, <embed> for anything else.
  • Canvas is a pixel surface painted with JavaScript; SVG is a set of shape tags that stay sharp at any size.
  • A domain name is rented through a registrar and resolved by DNS; web hosting is the rented space on a permanently connected server.
  • CSS attaches in three ways: inline (one element), embedded (one page) and external (the whole site) — and in a clash, inline beats embedded beats external.

Answers to Group B

1. A browser is application software installed on the user's device; a search engine is a website reached through a browser. A browser fetches and renders one page you name; a search engine returns a ranked list of pages matching a query. A browser uses a rendering engine; a search engine uses a crawler, an indexer and a ranking algorithm. A browser needs no internet connection to open a local file; a search engine always does. Examples: Chrome, Firefox, Edge against Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo.

2. A tag is the keyword in angle brackets that names an HTML element, usually in a pair such as <p> … </p>. An attribute is extra information written inside the opening tag as name="value" that modifies the element. In <img src="everest.jpg" alt="Everest" width="300">, img is the tag and src, alt and width are attributes. Four empty tags: <br>, <hr>, <img>, <meta> (also <link>, <input>, <source>).

5. CSS is the language that describes how HTML elements are presented — colour, size, spacing and typeface. Inline: a style attribute on one tag, <p style="color:green">Text</p>, styling that element only. Embedded: a <style> element in the <head>, <style> h1 { color: navy; } </style>, styling that page. External: rules in a separate .css file linked with <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css"> in the <head>, styling every page that links to it. In a clash, inline beats embedded, which beats external.

6. A domain name is the unique human-readable address of a website, such as neb.gov.np, resolved to an IP address by DNS; it is rented from a registrar and renewed periodically. Web hosting is the service of storing the site's files on a server that is permanently connected to the internet. The domain is the address; the hosting is the land and building at that address. They are bought separately and joined by pointing the domain at the host's name servers.

3. (a) Canvas is a raster (pixel) surface, SVG is vector (shapes). Canvas is drawn by JavaScript, SVG by tags written in the HTML. Enlarging a canvas drawing makes it blurry, SVG stays sharp at any size. Canvas forgets the shapes once they are painted, so nothing can be clicked or restyled, while every SVG shape stays in the document tree and can be styled with CSS or given an event. Canvas suits games and charts with very many points; SVG suits logos, icons and diagrams.

<video> creates the player; controls shows the play/pause bar and poster gives the still image displayed before playing. Each <source> offers one file format, and the browser uses the first one it can decode, ignoring the others. <track> attaches the WebVTT subtitle file, kind="subtitles" says what kind of text it is, srclang="en" its language and default selects it automatically. The sentence before </video> is fallback text, shown only by a browser that does not support the element at all.
